## Learn

- [Learn](https://shivamthakur.me/learn): free learning hub.
- [DSA Master: Data Structures & Algorithms in JavaScript](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master): DSA Master is a free, 28-chapter course that teaches data structures and algorithms in JavaScript from first principles. Each chapter explains one topic with real-life analogies, dry runs and runnable code, then ends with revision notes, a cheat sheet, 20 MCQs, 20 coding problems, interview questions and project ideas.
- [Chapter 1: Big-O Notation and Time Complexity in JavaScript](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/big-o-notation-time-complexity): Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's running time or memory grows as the input grows, ignoring constants and machine speed. This chapter explains what data structures and algorithms are, why we measure growth instead of timing code, every common complexity class from O(1) to O(n!), and the real cost of JavaScript's built-in methods.
- [Chapter 2: Recursion in JavaScript: Call Stack, Base Cases and Memoization](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/recursion-in-javascript): Recursion is a technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem until it reaches a base case. This chapter covers the anatomy of a recursive function, what happens on the call stack, why naive Fibonacci is exponential, how memoization fixes it, and when iteration is the better choice.
- [Chapter 3: Arrays and Strings in JavaScript: Two Pointers, Sliding Window and Prefix Sums](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/arrays-and-strings-javascript): Arrays store elements in contiguous memory, which gives O(1) access by index, while JavaScript strings are immutable sequences of characters. This chapter explains how dynamic arrays grow, the true cost of every array operation, and the four patterns that solve most array and string problems: two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums and difference arrays.
- [Chapter 4: Hashing in JavaScript: Hash Tables, Map, Set and Collisions](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/hashing-hash-table-javascript): A hash table stores key-value pairs by running each key through a hash function that computes where it belongs, which gives O(1) average lookup, insertion and deletion. This chapter builds a hash table from scratch, explains collisions, chaining, open addressing and resizing, compares Object, Map, Set and WeakMap, and teaches the five hashing patterns used in interviews.
- [Chapter 5: Linked Lists in JavaScript: Singly, Doubly and Circular](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/linked-list-javascript): A linked list is a sequence of nodes where each node stores a value and a pointer to the next node, so elements do not need to sit next to each other in memory. This chapter builds singly and doubly linked lists in JavaScript, compares them with arrays, and works through the classic problems: reversal, merging, middle node, cycle detection and removal.
- [Chapter 6: Stacks and Queues in JavaScript: LIFO, FIFO and Deques](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/stack-and-queue-javascript): A stack is a last-in-first-out (LIFO) collection where you add and remove from the same end; a queue is first-in-first-out (FIFO), adding at the back and removing from the front. This chapter implements both in JavaScript, introduces the deque, explains why Array.shift makes a slow queue, and shows where these structures power real software.
- [Chapter 7: Fast and Slow Pointers: Floyd's Cycle Detection Explained](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/fast-and-slow-pointers): The fast and slow pointer technique moves two pointers through a sequence at different speeds, usually one step and two steps at a time. If there is a cycle the fast pointer eventually meets the slow one. This chapter proves why Floyd's algorithm works, finds the cycle's start and length, and applies the pattern to arrays, numbers and palindrome lists.
- [Chapter 8: Trees in JavaScript: Binary Trees, Traversals and Binary Search Trees](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/binary-tree-and-bst-javascript): A tree is a hierarchical structure of nodes where each node has children and exactly one parent, except the root. A binary search tree keeps smaller values on the left and larger values on the right, which allows O(log n) search when it is balanced. This chapter covers tree vocabulary, the four traversal orders, recursive tree metrics, BST operations and self-balancing trees.
- [Chapter 9: Heaps and Priority Queues in JavaScript: Min-Heap, Max-Heap and Top-K](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/heap-priority-queue-javascript): A heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array where every parent is smaller (min-heap) or larger (max-heap) than its children, so the minimum or maximum is always at the top. This chapter builds a generic heap in JavaScript, explains sift-up, sift-down and O(n) heapify, and covers the Top-K and two-heap median patterns.
- [Chapter 10: Trie Data Structure in JavaScript: Prefix Trees and Autocomplete](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/trie-data-structure): A trie, or prefix tree, stores strings character by character so that words with the same prefix share the same path from the root. It answers prefix questions, such as which words start with a given prefix, in time proportional to the prefix length. This chapter builds a trie in JavaScript and applies it to autocomplete, word break and grid word search.
- [Chapter 11: Graphs in JavaScript: Adjacency Lists, BFS and DFS](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/graph-bfs-dfs-javascript): A graph is a set of vertices connected by edges, and it can model networks, maps, dependencies and social connections. This chapter covers graph vocabulary and types, how to represent a graph with an adjacency list or matrix, depth-first and breadth-first search with visited tracking, connected components, grid problems and cycle detection in directed and undirected graphs.
- [Chapter 12: Shortest Path Algorithms: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/shortest-path-dijkstra-bellman-ford): Shortest path algorithms find the cheapest route between vertices in a weighted graph. Dijkstra's algorithm is fastest for non-negative weights, Bellman-Ford handles negative weights and detects negative cycles, and Floyd-Warshall computes the distance between every pair of vertices. This chapter implements all three in JavaScript and gives a decision framework for choosing between them.
- [Chapter 13: Topological Sort and Minimum Spanning Trees: Kahn's, Kruskal's and Prim's](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/topological-sort-minimum-spanning-tree): Topological sort orders the vertices of a directed acyclic graph so that every dependency comes before what depends on it, as in build systems and course schedules. A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices of a weighted graph with the smallest total edge cost. This chapter implements Kahn's algorithm, DFS-based topological sort, Kruskal's algorithm and Prim's algorithm.
- [Chapter 14: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) in JavaScript: Path Compression and Union by Rank](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/union-find-disjoint-set): Union-Find, also called disjoint set union (DSU), keeps track of which elements belong to the same group and can merge two groups or check whether two elements are connected almost instantly. This chapter builds it in JavaScript, then adds union by rank and path compression, which together bring each operation down to amortized O(α(n)), effectively constant time.
- [Chapter 15: Sorting Algorithms in JavaScript: Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Heap Sort and More](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/sorting-algorithms-javascript): Sorting algorithms put elements in order, and they differ in speed, memory use and stability. This chapter implements bubble, selection and insertion sort, then merge sort, quick sort and heap sort, and finally counting and radix sort, which beat the O(n log n) limit for comparison sorts. It also explains how JavaScript's Array.prototype.sort works under the hood.
- [Chapter 16: Binary Search Patterns: Boundaries, Rotated Arrays and Binary Search on the Answer](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/binary-search-patterns): Binary search finds a target in sorted data by halving the search range at every step, which takes O(log n) time. Its real power is broader: any problem with a monotonic yes/no condition can be binary searched. This chapter covers correct boundary handling, first and last occurrence, rotated sorted arrays, binary search on the answer and searching 2D matrices.
- [Chapter 17: Backtracking in JavaScript: Permutations, Combinations, N-Queens and Sudoku](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/backtracking-algorithms): Backtracking builds a solution one choice at a time and undoes the last choice as soon as it cannot lead to a valid answer. Every backtracking algorithm follows the same choose, explore and un-choose template over a decision tree. This chapter applies that template to permutations, combinations, combination sum, N-Queens, Sudoku and word search, with pruning to cut the search.
- [Chapter 18: Dynamic Programming in JavaScript, Part 1: One-Dimensional DP](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/dynamic-programming-1d): Dynamic programming solves a problem by breaking it into overlapping sub-problems, solving each one only once and reusing the stored answers. It applies when a problem has optimal substructure and overlapping sub-problems. This chapter teaches a five-step framework for any DP problem, compares top-down memoization with bottom-up tabulation, and works through four classic one-dimensional problems.
- [Chapter 19: Dynamic Programming in JavaScript, Part 2: Two-Dimensional DP](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/dynamic-programming-2d): Two-dimensional dynamic programming uses a table indexed by two values, such as positions in two strings or an item and a remaining capacity. This chapter applies the same five-step DP framework to grid path counting, longest common subsequence, edit distance and the 0/1 knapsack problem, and shows how to reduce each table to a single row.
- [Chapter 20: Greedy Algorithms in JavaScript: When the Local Best Is the Global Best](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/greedy-algorithms): A greedy algorithm builds a solution by always taking the choice that looks best right now, never reconsidering it. It is only correct when the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. This chapter shows where greedy fails, how to prove it correct with an exchange argument, and works through activity selection, interval scheduling, Huffman coding and greedy versus DP.
- [Chapter 21: Monotonic Stack and Monotonic Queue in JavaScript](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/monotonic-stack-and-queue): A monotonic stack keeps its elements in increasing or decreasing order by popping anything that would break the order before pushing. That turns next-greater and next-smaller element problems from O(n²) into O(n). This chapter works through daily temperatures and largest rectangle in a histogram, then uses a monotonic deque to solve sliding window maximum in linear time.
- [Chapter 22: String Algorithms in JavaScript: KMP, Rabin-Karp and Suffix Structures](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/string-algorithms-kmp-rabin-karp): String matching algorithms find occurrences of a pattern inside a text faster than checking every position from scratch. KMP uses a precomputed LPS array so the text pointer never moves backwards, giving O(n + m) time, while Rabin-Karp compares rolling hashes of each window. This chapter implements both in JavaScript and introduces suffix arrays and suffix trees.
- [Chapter 23: Segment Trees and Fenwick Trees in JavaScript: Range Queries and Updates](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/segment-tree-fenwick-tree): Segment trees and Fenwick trees answer range queries, such as the sum or minimum of a subarray, while also allowing the array to change, with both operations in O(log n). This chapter builds a segment tree using the no, total and partial overlap cases, builds a compact Fenwick tree with the lowest-set-bit trick, and extends both to range updates.
- [Chapter 24: Bit Manipulation and Bitmask Dynamic Programming in JavaScript](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/bit-manipulation-bitmask-dp): Bit manipulation works directly on the binary digits of integers, which makes some operations far faster and smaller in memory. This chapter is a complete reference to JavaScript's bitwise operators and their 32-bit behaviour, a toolkit of bit tricks such as XOR cancellation and clearing the lowest set bit, how to represent sets as bitmasks, and bitmask dynamic programming.
- [Chapter 25: Mathematics for Programmers: Number Theory, Combinatorics and Game Theory](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/math-for-programmers-number-theory): Many algorithm problems rest on a small amount of mathematics. This chapter covers the number theory programmers use most (GCD and LCM with the Euclidean algorithm, primality testing, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, modular arithmetic and fast exponentiation), the combinatorics behind permutations, combinations and Pascal's triangle, and an introduction to game theory through Nim and the Sprague-Grundy theorem.
- [Chapter 26: Advanced Graph Theory: Bipartite Matching, Maximum Flow and Min-Cut](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/advanced-graph-algorithms-network-flow): Network flow algorithms find the maximum amount that can move from a source to a sink through a graph whose edges have capacities. This chapter starts with bipartite graphs and bipartite matching, builds the Ford-Fulkerson method and the Edmonds-Karp algorithm on a residual graph, and explains the max-flow min-cut theorem and how to recover the minimum cut.
- [Chapter 27: DSA for System Design: LRU Cache, Rate Limiting, B-Trees and Consistent Hashing](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/dsa-for-system-design): The data structures used in coding interviews are the same ones inside real production systems. This chapter connects them: an LRU cache built from a hash map and a doubly linked list, sliding-window and token-bucket rate limiters, B-trees behind database indexes, consistent hashing for load balancing, and distributed concepts such as Bloom filters.
- [Chapter 28: DSA Interview Preparation: Patterns, 90-Day Roadmap and Top 100 Problems](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/dsa-interview-preparation-roadmap): This chapter is the revision index for the whole DSA Master series. It maps problem statements to the right technique, collects every complexity in one reference table, lists the 100 most asked interview problems organized by pattern, and gives a pattern decision tree, 90-day and 180-day study plans, a mock interview protocol and a complete glossary.
- [Backend Master: Node.js, Databases, Security and System Design](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master): Backend Master is a free, 36-chapter course that takes you from how the internet works to designing and operating a production backend. It teaches Node.js, REST and GraphQL APIs, PostgreSQL, MongoDB and Redis, authentication and security, testing, caching, queues, scaling, Docker, CI/CD and system design through one running e-commerce project called ShopLine. Chapters 1 to 28 show real, executed code with the output we measured; later chapters are clearly labelled where examples were not run.
- [Backend Master Chapter 1: What Is Backend Development? The Big Picture](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/what-is-backend-development): Backend development is building the programs that run on servers, store data and answer requests from browsers and apps. This chapter explains the client-server model, what happens between a click and a response, what a backend developer is responsible for, and introduces ShopLine, the e-commerce project used throughout the course.
- [Backend Master Chapter 2: How the Internet Works: IP, DNS, TCP, TLS and Latency](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/how-the-internet-works-dns-tcp-tls): Every request your backend serves travels over IP, is routed using DNS, carried by TCP and protected by TLS. This chapter explains each layer with measured examples, the latency numbers that govern performance, and what really happens between typing a URL and seeing a page.
- [Backend Master Chapter 3: HTTP Explained: Methods, Status Codes, Headers, Cookies and Caching](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/http-explained-methods-status-codes-headers): HTTP is the request-response protocol every web API speaks. This chapter covers requests and responses on the wire, safe and idempotent methods, the status code families, essential headers, cookies, caching and the differences between HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, with runnable examples.
- [Backend Master Chapter 4: Linux, the Terminal, Git and Your Backend Dev Environment](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/linux-terminal-git-for-backend-developers): Most backends run on Linux and are managed from a terminal, with Git tracking every change. This chapter teaches the commands, permissions, processes, environment variables, SSH basics and Git workflow a backend developer uses daily.
- [Backend Master Chapter 5: Node.js Internals: The Event Loop, Streams, Worker Threads and Cluster](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/nodejs-event-loop-streams-worker-threads): Node.js runs your JavaScript on one thread and delegates I/O to the operating system and a thread pool. This chapter explains the event loop phases, microtasks, why blocking code freezes every request, streams and backpressure, worker threads for CPU work and the cluster module, with measured examples.
- [Backend Master Chapter 6: Your First Real Server: Node.js HTTP, Routing, Middleware and Express](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/nodejs-http-server-routing-middleware-express): A backend server is a program that listens on a port and turns requests into responses. This chapter builds one with Node's http module, then Express, covering routing, middleware order, error handling and project structure, and creates the first ShopLine endpoints.
- [Backend Master Chapter 7: Express 5 and Fastify: Zod Validation, Security Middleware and Uploads](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/express-5-fastify-validation-zod-security-middleware): Production APIs validate every input, add security headers, limit abuse and log structured events. This chapter covers Express 5 changes, Zod schemas, helmet, CORS, rate limiting, pino logging, file uploads with multer and the Fastify framework, including bugs found by testing.
- [Backend Master Chapter 8: REST API Design: Resources, Pagination, Idempotency, Versioning and OpenAPI](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/rest-api-design-pagination-idempotency-versioning): A good REST API is predictable, safe to retry and easy to evolve. This chapter covers resource naming, cursor pagination, filtering, idempotency keys, optimistic concurrency with ETags, versioning, consistent problem+json errors and documenting the contract with OpenAPI.
- [Backend Master Chapter 9: GraphQL with Node.js: Schemas, Resolvers, DataLoader and Query Limits](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/graphql-api-nodejs-dataloader-security): GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need from a single endpoint. This chapter covers schemas and resolvers, the N+1 query problem and per-request DataLoader batching, defences against expensive queries, authorization and how to decide between GraphQL and REST.
- [Backend Master Chapter 10: Real-Time Communication: SSE, WebSockets, Webhooks and gRPC in Node.js](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/sse-websockets-webhooks-grpc-nodejs): Not every interaction fits request and response. This chapter compares server-sent events, WebSockets, webhooks and gRPC, shows how to build and test each in Node.js, and covers reconnection, heartbeats, signed and idempotent webhook handling and when to pick which.
- [Backend Master Chapter 11: Backend Architecture Patterns: Layers, Dependency Injection and the Modular Monolith](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/backend-architecture-patterns-modular-monolith): Architecture decides how easy a backend is to change and test. This chapter builds ShopLine with controllers, services and repositories, a composition root for dependency injection, hexagonal ports and adapters and a modular monolith whose boundaries are enforced by tests.
- [Backend Master Chapter 12: Database Fundamentals: ACID, CAP, MVCC and How Data Lives on Disk](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/database-fundamentals-acid-cap-mvcc): Databases exist because files cannot safely handle concurrent updates. This chapter demonstrates a lost-update bug with a JSON file, then explains ACID, write-ahead logging, pages and B-trees, MVCC, the CAP and PACELC trade-offs, connection pooling and SQL injection on a real PostgreSQL.
- [Backend Master Chapter 13: SQL Mastery with PostgreSQL: From SELECT to Joins, CTEs and Window Functions](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/postgresql-sql-tutorial-joins-window-functions): SQL is the language of relational data. This chapter teaches PostgreSQL from SELECT to joins, anti-joins, CTEs including recursive ones, window functions and JSONB, shows the traps that produce wrong numbers (NULLs and join fan-out), and covers safe Node.js patterns such as parameters and keyset pagination.
- [Backend Master Chapter 14: Schema Design and Normalization: Keys, Constraints and Zero-Downtime Migrations](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/database-schema-design-normalization-migrations): A good schema makes wrong data impossible. This chapter reproduces the update, delete and insert anomalies, fixes them with normalization, models one-to-many and many-to-many relationships, adds soft delete and audit triggers, and shows a tested migration runner plus which ALTER TABLE operations are safe on large tables.
- [Backend Master Chapter 15: PostgreSQL Indexes and Query Performance: Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/postgresql-indexes-explain-analyze-query-performance): Indexes turn full table scans into a few page reads. On a one-million-row table this chapter measures an index cutting a query from 107 ms to 0.28 ms, shows how to read EXPLAIN ANALYZE, explains why the planner sometimes ignores an index, and covers composite, covering, partial, expression, GIN and BRIN indexes, the N+1 problem and pg_stat_statements.
- [Backend Master Chapter 16: Transactions, Isolation Levels and Concurrency Control in PostgreSQL](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/database-transactions-isolation-levels-concurrency): Concurrency bugs are silent and costly. This chapter runs 50 simultaneous buyers against a 10-item stock to show a naive read-modify-write confirming 50 orders, then fixes it six ways, demonstrates isolation anomalies including write skew, row locks and SKIP LOCKED queues, deadlocks and the correct transaction pattern in Node.js.
- [Backend Master Chapter 17: ORMs and Query Builders: Knex, Kysely, Drizzle and Prisma Compared](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/orm-vs-query-builder-prisma-drizzle-knex-kysely): ORMs and query builders trade control for convenience but never remove the need to understand SQL. This chapter runs the same feature through Knex, Kysely, Drizzle and Prisma, prints the SQL each generates, compares eager loading, transactions and type handling, and gives a decision checklist.
- [Backend Master Chapter 18: MongoDB and Document Modeling: Embedding, Indexes, Aggregation and Mongoose](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/mongodb-data-modeling-aggregation-mongoose): MongoDB stores flexible JSON-like documents but still needs careful design. This chapter covers BSON, embedding versus referencing, compound and TTL indexes with explain output on 200,000 documents, the aggregation pipeline, atomic updates and transactions, schema validation, Mongoose, and the traps: operator injection and the 16 MB limit.
- [Backend Master Chapter 19: Redis and In-Memory Data: Caching, Rate Limiting, Locks and Streams](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/redis-tutorial-caching-rate-limiting-streams): Redis is an in-memory data-structure server that is fast because it is single-threaded and keeps data in RAM. This chapter covers its data structures, cache-aside with stampede protection, atomic rate limiting with Lua, safe distributed locks, pub/sub versus streams, what survives a crash, and eviction, with a tested lab.
- [Backend Master Chapter 20: Other Data Stores: Search, Time-Series, Analytics and Object Storage](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/full-text-search-time-series-olap-object-storage): Every extra data store is a copy that must be kept in sync. This chapter measures PostgreSQL full-text search against ILIKE, tries Elasticsearch, shows partitioning and columnar analytics with DuckDB, explains object storage and presigned uploads, and gives a framework for deciding when PostgreSQL is enough.
- [Backend Master Chapter 21: Authentication: Password Hashing, Sessions, JWT, Refresh Tokens, OAuth and MFA](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/authentication-passwords-sessions-jwt-oauth-mfa): Authentication proves who a user is. This chapter measures why SHA-256 is wrong for passwords and argon2id is right, builds cookie sessions and short-lived JWTs with rotating refresh tokens and reuse detection, implements TOTP verified against the RFC vectors, explains OAuth with PKCE, and attacks each piece to show why the defences exist.
- [Backend Master Chapter 22: Authorization and Access Control: RBAC, IDOR, Mass Assignment and Row-Level Security](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/authorization-rbac-idor-row-level-security): Authorization decides what an authenticated user may do, and broken access control is the top web vulnerability. This chapter attacks a small API with IDOR, a missing role check and mass assignment, fixes each, builds a central default-deny policy function, and enforces tenant isolation with PostgreSQL row-level security and its three traps.
- [Backend Master Chapter 23: Web and API Security: XSS, CSRF, SSRF, CORS, Injection and Hardening](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/web-api-security-xss-csrf-ssrf-cors-owasp): Most web vulnerabilities come from treating data as code. This chapter runs vulnerable and fixed routes side by side for XSS, path traversal, command injection, SSRF, open redirects, CORS, CSRF, prototype pollution and ReDoS, adds security headers with helmet, and covers limits, secrets and dependency risk against the OWASP Top 10.
- [Backend Master Chapter 24: Backend Testing Strategy: Unit, Integration, Property-Based and Mutation Tests](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/backend-testing-strategy-node-test-integration-property): More tests and higher coverage do not guarantee a safe backend. This chapter builds a 25-test suite with the built-in node:test runner and a real PostgreSQL, shows a property test finding a negative order total, a mock hiding a broken SQL update, a flaky timing test, 99.6 percent coverage with surviving mutants, and a load test.
- [Backend Master Chapter 25: Logging, Monitoring, Tracing and Debugging a Live Node.js Service](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/logging-monitoring-tracing-nodejs-observability): You cannot attach a debugger to production, so the system must explain itself. This chapter builds structured logs with correlation ids and redaction, RED metrics with route labels, a trace across two services, liveness and readiness checks, SLO maths, and diagnoses event-loop blocking, a memory leak and a CPU hotspot.
- [Backend Master Chapter 26: Error Handling and Resilience: Timeouts, Retries, Circuit Breakers and Bulkheads](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/error-handling-resilience-retries-circuit-breaker): Everything fails, so resilience is what the system does next. This chapter builds a small toolkit and tests it against simulated failing dependencies: timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, the retry storm, a circuit breaker, a bulkhead that kept an unrelated endpoint fast, and why retries without idempotency keys caused extra charges.
- [Backend Master Chapter 27: Caching: HTTP Cache-Control, ETags, Redis Cache-Aside and Invalidation](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/caching-strategies-http-cache-redis-invalidation): Caching trades freshness for speed and load reduction, and every cache is a copy that can drift. This chapter tests HTTP caching with validators and stale-while-revalidate through a small shared cache, measures a 78 times faster Redis hit, reproduces the stale-write race and fixes it with versioned keys, and compares eviction policies.
- [Backend Master Chapter 28: Asynchronous Processing: Message Queues, Background Jobs and the Outbox Pattern](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/message-queues-background-jobs-outbox-nodejs): Slow or flaky work should not run inside the HTTP request. This chapter builds a PostgreSQL job queue with leases and fenced completion, compares BullMQ and Redis Streams, tests crashes, poison jobs and duplicate delivery, shows the outbox pattern avoiding silent event loss, and covers backpressure and cron on several instances.
- [Backend Master Chapter 29: Scaling and Load Balancing: Stateless Services, nginx, PgBouncer and Read Replicas](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/scaling-backend-load-balancing-nginx-pgbouncer): Scaling mostly means removing what stops you adding a second server, usually state. This chapter puts three Node instances behind nginx, measures algorithms, failover, sessions and throughput scaling, shows PgBouncer serving 300 clients with 10 database connections and its session-state trap, and explains read replicas and autoscaling.
- [Backend Master Chapter 30: Distributed Systems: CAP, Consistency, Consensus, Consistent Hashing and Sagas](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/distributed-systems-cap-raft-consensus-sagas): Once a system spans machines, partial failure, unreliable networks and clocks become unavoidable. This chapter explains CAP and PACELC, consistency models, quorums, split-brain, Raft, consistent hashing, fencing tokens, two-phase commit versus sagas and CRDTs. It was written without running the code sketches, which are marked not run.
- [Backend Master Chapter 31: Docker and Containers for Node.js: Dockerfile, Compose, Signals and Kubernetes Basics](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/docker-for-nodejs-dockerfile-compose-kubernetes): A container packages your application with its runtime so it runs the same everywhere. This chapter explains what containers are, writes a production Dockerfile with multi-stage builds, a non-root user and tini, a Compose file for the local stack, signals and graceful shutdown, resource limits, security hardening and Kubernetes basics. The Dockerfiles and manifests were not run.
- [Backend Master Chapter 32: CI/CD and Cloud Basics: GitHub Actions, Deployment Strategies and Safe Migrations](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/ci-cd-github-actions-deployment-strategies-cloud): Small, frequent, automated and reversible releases are safer than big manual ones. This chapter shows a CI pipeline with a real database, build-once promotion, rolling, blue/green and canary strategies, expand and contract migrations in deploys, feature flags and rollbacks, infrastructure as code, and a map of cloud services. The workflows were not run.
- [Backend Master Chapter 33: Microservices vs Monolith: Choosing Your Architecture and Migrating Safely](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/microservices-vs-monolith-architecture-decision): Microservices buy independent deployment and team autonomy at the cost of network failures, eventual consistency and operational complexity. This chapter compares the options, argues for a modular monolith by default, gives a decision framework, covers boundaries, data ownership, communication and the strangler fig migration. It contains no executed examples.
- [Backend Master Chapter 34: System Design for Backend Engineers: Framework, Estimation and Five Worked Designs](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/system-design-for-backend-engineers): System design is combining databases, caches, queues and load balancers to meet requirements with justified trade-offs. This chapter gives a repeatable framework and the numbers to estimate with, then works through a URL shortener, flash-sale checkout, notification service, distributed rate limiter and news feed. It contains no executed examples.
- [Backend Master Chapter 35: Capstone Project: Build and Operate a Production E-Commerce Backend](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/backend-capstone-project-build-ecommerce-api): The capstone assembles everything into one production-grade ShopLine backend. It gives the specification and quality bar, a modular monolith architecture, twelve milestones with acceptance criteria and chapter pointers, a testing plan, a 13-point review rubric, runbooks and architecture decision records. It is a plan, not tested code.
- [Backend Master Chapter 36: The Backend Mega Appendix: Cheat Sheets, Glossary, Interview Questions and Roadmap](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/backend-master/backend-cheat-sheets-glossary-interview-questions): This appendix collects the quick-reference material from the whole course: HTTP status codes and headers, REST conventions, SQL and PostgreSQL error codes, Node.js, Linux, Git, Docker, Redis and MongoDB one-pagers, a security checklist, decision tables, a glossary, an interview question bank, a roadmap and an honest ledger of what was tested.
